rationale: A wins because it more often turns the update into reportable assignments with real proof gates, especially “What ‘third-party verified’ actually means” and its demand for LCA boundaries, baseline, and report access. B has bones, but it keeps inflating “default non-dairy option” into a dairy displacement story; “One coffee chain just made dairy optional. Dairy is taking notice.” is a fact error wearing a trade-beat costume. A still needs surgery: “customers who don’t specify get oat milk” is not in the update and cannot go anywhere near a reporter until confirmed.
gaps_in_A: “customers who don’t specify get oat milk” overreads the fact. The update says Oatly becomes the default non-dairy option, not the default milk for all customers.

“falling volumes, shrinking retail shelf space, canceled expansions” imports a plant-based-sector narrative not present in the update. If you need that frame, it belongs in required proof, not asserted as fact.

“Cut a factory, win the café deal” and “Oatly is still losing money” overlap heavily around the same loss/plant-closure/partnership tension. One sharper business angle would beat two adjacent wrappers.
gaps_in_B: “One coffee chain just made dairy optional” is wrong on the supplied facts. Default non-dairy option does not mean dairy became optional.
“Dairy is taking notice” invents a reaction. No dairy trade group, competitor, farmer group, or market-share evidence appears in the update.
“When oat milk stops being the alternative and becomes the default pour” turns one unnamed regional chain into a category shift before proving a second example exists.
“a chain-wide default switch away from dairy changes ordering, training, and inventory at scale” smuggles in operational consequences the update does not state. Plausible is not the same as grounded.
